Complete positively documented two-person DJ-and-live-saxophone format, not a claim of exhaustive credits for any studio single. tradition.name: Pinoy Hip Hop
tradition.lineage: Ruby Ibarra — complete NPR Tiny Desk three-song concert, published29May2025. Detailed materials, instrument makes, playing presets, room, production chain and neutral axes are authored choices, not measured source-session facts. Bare keys retain source-unspecified architecture. Generic guitar/bass/flute credits are rendered as clean-strummed amplified guitar, fingerstyle electric bass and silver concert flute; source does not identify pickup, manufacturer or embouchure. Optional global tuning is omitted; vocal register/training/pitch mechanism remain source-unspecified.

extras.description: NPR producer Elle Mannion publishes the complete eight-person performance roster and all three songs: Bakunawa,7000 Miles,Someday. Ruby Ibarra and Ouida sing; June Millington sings and plays guitar; Anna Macan plays guitar and sings backing vocals; Camille Ramirez plays bass and flute and sings backing vocals; Angelo LASI Macaraeg plays keys and guitar; JoJo Gajardo Ramirez plays drums; Charito Soriano sings backing vocals. All six positively credited voices and six instrument families remain represented. The record distinguishes the performer roster from production staff and the audience. This complete2025 Tiny Desk programme is distinct from the earlier contest-submission recording. No Han Han guest credit from that different version is imported. Three credited guitarists share one authored guitar-family card; Camille’s bass and flute roles are preserved as a programme-union palette rather than an assertion that she plays both simultaneously. All six named voices are covered by a live group without invented contrapuntal voice parts. The act is a Filipino diaspora hip-hop practice: the broadcaster identifies an all-Filipino band, Tagalog/Bisaya/English rap and Philippine immigrant narratives, not merely a US act chosen through ethnic inference. Broad Filipino hip-hop practice includes Philippine and diaspora rappers using Filipino-language and cultural narratives. It is broader than existing pinoy_trap: this documented multilingual live-band concert does not require trap’s 808/hi-hat chassis. Existing pinoy_rnb centers sung R&B; selected performance positively centers rap with accompanying singers. No novel exclusive acoustic property or equivalence to the narrower alternative/drill labels is asserted. Exact materials, makes, playing settings, tuning, room, signal chain and axes are authored choices, not measured source-session facts or universal genre characteristics.

extras.description: Alexeyeff’s primary fieldwork paper describes recurring household gatherings on Rarotonga: family members sing and pass a ukulele between them, accompanied by spoon-in-beer-bottle and spatula-on-plastic-bowl percussion. Select that whole observed informal practice, retaining both found objects and unknown singer headcount. The paper directly identifies the surrounding repertoire as Cook Islands contemporary popular island music. This is a documented regional popular-song practice, not the neighboring unaccompanied Christian himene forms or a generic pre-contact Polynesian traditional category. The same primary study places island music in local and diasporic commercial circulation while observing its informal household realization; no commercial master arrangement is inferred. The source-scoped palette retains voice, ukulele and both named found percussion objects without adding the electric instruments discussed for other formal contexts. Category identification rests on primary ethnographic practice, not merely artist nationality or a different arrangement. The family’s actual singer and player headcounts are unspecified; one group-voice owner and one ukulele owner do not assert three singers or simultaneous ukulele players. Broad functionalSong uses the paper’s tonal/chordal song discussion as context, with authored chord-strummed realization; source timing, pitch intervals and exact ukulele construction remain unspecified. Existing four-string soprano mahogany ukulele is an explicitly authored hardware approximation, not a claim about the observed instrument or Hawaiian cultural identity. Neutral voice physiology and group ensemble defaults avoid guessing individuals. No global tuning is asserted. The isolated percussion owner includes both documented objects with no invented dimensions/material of the spoon, spatula or bottle. Numeric sound axes are authored routing choices, not acoustic measurements. No later stage band or album lineup is transferred to the household scene. tradition.name: Latin arena pop
tradition.lineage: Sin Bandera — Nunca (2026), complete released track. Representative authored present-day recording arrangement for the selected documented branch. Sources establish category, roles and locality. Exact materials, makes, playing settings, tuning, room, signal chain and axes are authored choices, not measured source-session facts or universal genre characteristics.

extras.description: Track 5 credits identify Leonel García and Noel Schajris as singers; García, Todd Lombardo and Daniel Vago Galindo on acoustic guitar; Schajris piano; Aaron Sterling drums; Mark Hill bass; Justin Ostrander electric guitar; Galindo and Alex Wright keyboards. All seven families and both singers retained. Generic keyboard identity remains distinct from explicitly credited piano, without guessing its generator. The creator category joins cross-border Spanish-language commercial pop performers around arena-scale touring and audience singalong repertoire; Sin Bandera appears at playlist item12 and its own biography documents Arena Monterrey and Auditorio Nacional concerts. Sin Bandera’s romantic-ballad branch positively overlaps existing latin_ballad and mexican_pop; their historical codification dates are not hard exclusions. The distinct requested category is instead the broader cross-border arena-pop discovery network, which also includes Mœnia (creator item22) and electronic-pop act Belanova (item30), plus rock band Maná (item68). Belanova’s own label describes an electropop dance-floor trio. Thus this network is not categorically equivalent to romantic ballad, nor to national Mexican pop: the same creator list includes Spain’s La Oreja de Van Gogh and Alejandro Sanz, and Guatemala’s Ricardo Arjona. The selected Sin Bandera ballad is one overlapping, fully documented branch, not the evidence that every arena-pop artist plays ballads. It does not redefine all Latin pop, imply the selected studio track was recorded at an arena, or claim every category member uses this lineup. Primary song text marks verses, chorus and bridge; artist account describes composing from harmonic sequences. Functional harmonization and the recipe playing settings are authored choices rather than a measured transcription. Three credited acoustic guitar players and two keyboard players aggregate into their family cards, without omitting people. Authored clean-strummed humbucker, fingerpicked OM, fingerstyle four-string-neutral electric bass, acoustic kit and nine-foot Steinway piano are timbral realizations, not credited makes or measured source technique. Both recorded singers are represented as a duet; live-ensemble stack is an authored combined vocal presentation, not a claim of simultaneous unoverdubbed studio recording. Creator membership establishes the broader category; the label establishes this complete acoustic branch. extras.description: The organizer-supplied official ticket program distinctly schedules an Interlude by Aycan Yeter and Erwan Keravec in the B3 foyer, between the two Sonneurs concert sections. It identifies Yeter as the traditional Turkish tulum player; the presenting institution Berliner Festspiele identifies Keravec as a Highland bagpipe player. The selected announced duo therefore retains tulum and Highland bagpipes with no sung part. This is a realization of the published instrumental encounter, not an assertion of a reviewed concert recording. The creator-owned Tulum playlist includes Aycan Yeter, positively anchoring this label to the Black Sea bagpipe music rather than the Mexican resort or house-music marketing term. Tulum foregrounds the instrument repertoire, while existing Karadeniz Türküleri covers broader regional songs and dance music; their intersection is acknowledged without declaring equivalence. The full separately titled duo Interlude is the scope, not an arbitrary removal of members from the Sonneurs quartet. No bombard, biniou, trelombard or electronics from separately programmed works is silently omitted from this duo or imported into it. No singing is assigned from Yeter’s separate vocal projects. The selected concert encounter is authored as modal elaboration around a sustained frame under improvOnFrame; this is a practical structural realization, not a measured score or an assertion that all tulum repertoire is improvised. Hemşin/Rize tulum with a free-air preset is an explicitly authored Eastern Black Sea branch, not a claim of the exact instrument seen at Arter or Yeter’s ethnicity. Goatskin/cane tulum and blackwood Highland pipes with cane reeds and hide bag are authored compatible material choices. Highland drone/outdoor-ceremonial descriptor is inherited from its physical three-drone card, not a claim the indoor interlude was a ceremony. Global tuning is omitted because the two bagpipe traditions do not have a source-documented shared temperament. instrument_role_audit.rationale: The presenting collective Eastern Margins, collaborating with Mixcloud, directly identifies and embeds this entire Hoàng Anh DJ mix as Vinahouse. Its first-person account places the genre in Vietnam and describes processed Vietnamese folk/VPop vocal material and energetic synth-led dance music. This is positive evidence of an actual DJ performance, not inference of sampler hardware from an opaque studio master. The scope is the complete linked DJ mix, not the separate six-hour Worldwide Vibe livestream announced in the same feature or other featured DJs. All embedded instrumental, vocal and effect content remains in source-unspecified DJ playback/mixing. Track count, duration, medium, deck count and processing hardware are unverified. Country geography marks the documented Vietnamese practice, not a claimed mix recording location.
